Trying to Conceive

Preconception Appointment: What to Expect and Ask

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A preconception appointment is a checkup with an OB-GYN, family physician, or midwife, ideally about three months before you start trying, where you review your health history, medicines, vaccines, and any tests worth doing before pregnancy. Most of it is conversation, and you leave with a short plan instead of a stack of orders. Here is how the visit usually unfolds, and the questions worth bringing with you.

Who to book with and when

You do not need a specialist to get started. An OB-GYN, a family physician, or a midwife can all run a preconception visit, so book with whoever already knows you best. When you call, say the words preconception checkup or preconception counseling so the clinic books enough time; a rushed ten-minute slot is not the goal here. If you do not have a regular clinician, this is a good reason to find one, because the same person will often care for you in early pregnancy. Partners are welcome at these visits too, and their history matters.

Aim to book about three months before you plan to start trying. That window is not arbitrary. Some changes need lead time: a vaccine may have a waiting period, a medicine may need a gradual switch, and a chronic condition may need a few weeks of tighter control. If you are already trying, do not skip the visit; it is still useful at any point. And if pregnancy is a year or more away, an ordinary annual exam is a fine place to mention your plans and ask what to do when the time gets closer.

Your health history, front and center

Most of the appointment is a conversation, not an exam. Expect questions about your periods and cycle length, past pregnancies and how they went, surgeries, current conditions, mental health, and any family history of genetic conditions, birth defects, blood clots, or early heart disease on either side. None of this is a test you can fail. The clinician is looking for anything worth planning around, and honest answers about smoking, alcohol, or a condition you have been ignoring get you better advice, not a lecture. Jot the key dates down before you go so you are not reconstructing them from memory in the room.

If you live with a chronic condition such as diabetes, high blood pressure, thyroid disease, asthma, epilepsy, or depression, this visit is where the pregnancy plan starts. Conditions that are well controlled before conception tend to cause fewer problems during pregnancy, so the clinician may suggest a check of your current numbers, a treatment adjustment, or a referral to the specialist who manages the condition. Ask directly: is my condition stable enough to start trying, what target are we aiming for first, and how will my care change once I am pregnant? Getting those answers now is much calmer than getting them at eight weeks.

Medicines, supplements, and vaccines

Bring a list of everything you take: prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products, with doses if you know them. The clinician will scan the list for anything that needs a closer look before pregnancy and flag what should be reviewed, switched, or continued. You do not need the full answer in this one visit; some changes get their own follow-up. The one rule to leave with is simple: do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own because you are trying to conceive. Untreated conditions carry risks too, and a planned switch is almost always safer than a sudden stop.

The vaccine review is one of the most concrete parts of the visit. Your clinician will check whether you are up to date on routine vaccines and may order a blood test if your records are missing. The timing rule matters here: the CDC advises that live vaccines, such as MMR and varicella, be given at least one month before conception, because they are not recommended during pregnancy. Non-live vaccines, such as the flu shot, can be given at any point, before or during pregnancy, so they rarely affect your timeline. If you need a live vaccine, this is exactly why the appointment works best a few months out.

Tests you might be offered

Expect a short list of blood and urine tests rather than a big workup. Common ones include immunity checks for rubella and varicella, your blood type and Rh factor, and screening for sexually transmitted infections such as HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, and chlamydia. Depending on your history, the clinician might add a blood count to look for anemia, a blood sugar or thyroid check, or a Pap test if you are due for one. Nothing on this list requires a hospital visit; most of it comes from one blood draw and a urine sample, often done the same day.

Carrier screening is worth raising even if no one offers it first. It is a blood or saliva test that checks whether you carry a gene change for conditions such as cystic fibrosis or spinal muscular atrophy, and ACOG recommends that it be offered to everyone who is pregnant or planning a pregnancy. Doing it before conception gives you the most options, because if you are a carrier, your partner can be tested next and you have time to talk through what the results mean. It is optional, usually a one-time test, and a genetic counselor can help you interpret anything unexpected.

Questions worth bringing with you

A short written list keeps the visit on track when the room feels rushed. Good questions to bring: Is anything in my health history worth sorting out before I start trying? Do any of my medicines or supplements need a review? Am I due for any vaccines, and do any of them have a waiting period? Which tests do you recommend for me, and should we talk about carrier screening? Is there anything about my cycle or my family history that changes your advice? You will not need all of them, but having them written down means the important ones get asked.

Before you leave, ask what happens next: which results will come back, who will call you, and whether anything needs a follow-up visit. Then write the plan down while it is fresh, including any dates, such as when a vaccine waiting period ends. A notes app, paper, or the BeMama app all work; the point is one place where the plan and your questions live. If new symptoms show up while you are trying, such as irregular bleeding, pelvic pain, or anything that worries you, contact your clinician rather than waiting for the next scheduled visit, and treat heavy bleeding or severe pain as a same-day call. This checkup is a starting point, not the last conversation.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Preconception guidance focuses on health history, medicines and supplements, vaccinations, chronic conditions, nutrition, substance use, and any previous pregnancy concerns. Changes are safest when planned with a qualified professional before pregnancy rather than made after a positive test.

For most people who could become pregnant, public-health guidance recommends 400 micrograms of folic acid daily beginning before conception. Individual needs differ, and prescribed medicines or higher-dose supplements should not be changed without professional advice.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to keep cycle dates, medicines, supplements, vaccination questions, and appointment notes together. The record can support a preconception conversation, but it cannot decide whether a medicine or supplement is safe.

When to seek help

Seek individualized advice before pregnancy if you have a chronic condition, use prescription medicine, had a previous pregnancy complication, or cannot stop alcohol, smoking, or another substance.

Sources and further reading

  • CDC — Medicine and Pregnancy: An Overview

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Book with an OB-GYN, family physician, or midwife about three months before you start trying.
  • Bring your health history, your family history, and a complete list of medicines and supplements.
  • Live vaccines like MMR and varicella need at least one month between the shot and conception.
  • Common tests include rubella and varicella immunity, blood type, and STI screening, and carrier screening is worth asking about.
  • Leave with a written plan, and contact your clinician if anything changes before your next visit.

Frequently asked questions

What happens at a preconception appointment?

A preconception appointment is mostly a structured conversation: your clinician reviews your personal and family health history, your medicines and supplements, and your vaccine record, then orders a few basic tests if needed. Many visits also touch on cycle tracking and carrier screening. You usually leave with a short list of actions rather than a diagnosis.

When should I schedule a preconception appointment?

About three months before you plan to start trying is a good target. That leaves time for vaccine waiting periods, medication changes, and getting a chronic condition steady. If you are already trying, book one anyway; the visit is useful at any stage.

Do I need a checkup before trying to get pregnant?

It is recommended, even if you feel completely healthy. Groups like ACOG and the CDC encourage preconception care because it catches things that are easier to fix before pregnancy, such as a missing vaccine or a thyroid level that needs adjusting. For most people, one visit is enough to build the plan.

What tests are done before getting pregnant?

Common preconception tests include blood checks for rubella and varicella immunity, your blood type and Rh factor, and screening for infections such as HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B. Depending on your history, a clinician may add a blood count, blood sugar, or thyroid test. Carrier screening for genetic conditions is optional and worth discussing.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
